failure.message: The visual review found 5 serious problems with how the scene is drawn or computed. You have not been charged. It was corrected automatically four times, but it still did not pass. Revise plan prepares a simpler plan from your request for you to review, using up to 56 AI credits; nothing is built until you press Generate.

plan.title: Stochastic gradient descent on a loss surface
plan.description: A long, narrow bowl-shaped surface stands for the loss (the error a model makes) over two weights. A ball starts high on the slope and steps downhill. At each step a thin arrow shows the true steepest-downhill direction. A thicker arrow shows the noisy estimate the ball actually follows, as if it came from a small random batch of data. The ball leaves a zigzag trail. You can change the step size and batch size, then compare the wobbly path of stochastic gradient descent with the smooth path of full-batch descent.
plan.reason: Stochastic gradient descent is about how noisy, cheap steps still get down to the bottom. Changing the step size and batch size while the path forms shows how noise and step size together shape that path.
interactions: Play, pause or advance one step at a time to watch the ball move.
Raise the learning rate to see longer steps. Near the top of the range the ball bounces back and forth across the narrow valley. Lower it to see slow, steady creeping.
Change the batch size: smaller batches make the step arrow swing further from the true downhill arrow and the trail more jagged. Full batch gives a smooth path.
Drag the ball to a new starting point on the surface before stepping.
Use 'Run again, keep old trail' to send the ball from the start point again while the previous path stays visible, faded, for comparison.
Read the step count, the current loss and the typical size of the gradient noise.
assumptions: Illustration: a made-up bowl-shaped loss with simulated gradient noise, not a real model trained on data.
The loss is half of (x² + 4y²). It is steep across the valley and gentle along it, so the bottom is at the center.

Each step moves the ball by minus the learning rate times the noisy gradient. The noisy gradient is the true gradient plus random noise whose size shrinks as one over the square root of the batch size. Full batch adds no noise.
The noise comes from the scene's fixed random seed, so after Reset the same sequence of noise is drawn again.
Each run stops after 300 steps. If a step would leave the drawn area, the ball is held at the edge.
The trail draws one marker every 5 steps, at most 60 markers; every step still runs.
limitations: Changed: the trail draws 60 markers, one every 5 steps, instead of 300; every step still runs.
Changed: the kept comparison path also draws at most 60 markers.
Single noisy steps can go uphill. The loss falls only on average, not at every step.
A real loss surface has millions of dimensions, plus flat regions and many low points. This one is a simple two-weight bowl with a single lowest point.
Fixed learning rates only: no momentum, no adaptive optimizers and no schedule that shrinks the step over time.
plan.learningGoal: Stochastic gradient descent follows a noisy estimate of the downhill direction. Smaller batches add more noise, and the step size controls both speed and stability. The loss still falls on average.

draft.title: Stochastic gradient descent on a narrow loss bowl
draft.description: A long, narrow bowl-shaped surface shows the loss over two weights. It is steep from left to right and gentle from front to back, and its lowest point is at the center. A red ball marks the current weights and steps downhill. A thin dark arrow shows the full-batch step, which points straight downhill. A thicker purple arrow shows the noisy step the ball actually takes. Both arrows are drawn at true size, so each tip marks where that step would land. An orange trail records the path. A faded blue path is an earlier run kept for comparison.
assumptions: Illustration: a made-up bowl-shaped loss with simulated gradient noise, not a real model trained on data.
Loss = ½(w1² + 4·w2²). w2 (steep) runs left to right, w1 (gentle) runs front to back, and the surface is drawn at a height of 0.25 × loss. The lowest point is at the center.

Step = −rate × (true gradient + noise). Each weight's noise has a std dev of 2/√batch. Full batch adds none. Across the valley each step multiplies w2 by 1 − 4·rate, so at 0.5 the ball bounces from side to side with no damping.
The noise comes from the fixed seed (7), so Reset replays the same noise. 'Run again' starts from the same point with new noise and keeps the old path faded.

A step that would leave the drawn area is held at the edge (status 'held at edge') and the run goes on. Converged = loss under 0.1 for 5 steps in a row; stopped = 300 steps done. A single noisy step can go uphill.
Changed from the plan: the trail marks every step (up to 300) instead of one marker every 5, so a side-to-side bounce stays visible. 10 steps per second.

Both arrows are steps (rate × gradient) drawn at one fixed scale of 1: across the ground each arrow is exactly as long as its step, tilted to follow the surface. Near the bottom the steps, and so the arrows, become very short.
Dragging the ball moves its start point across the valley (w2) only. The start along the valley stays at w1 = 2.2.

Draw each step as rate × gradient times one fixed, disclosed scale.

A step that would leave the drawn area is held at the edge (status 'held at edge') and the run goes on. Converged = loss under 0.1 for 5 steps in a row; stopped = 300 steps done. A single noisy step can go uphill.
Changed from the plan: the trail marks every step (up to 300) instead of one marker every 5, so a side-to-side bounce stays visible. 10 steps per second.

Both arrows are steps (rate × gradient) on one shared scale that changes each step: the longer spans 0.9 units across the ground and each tilts to stay above the surface, so directions and length ratio compare, not absolute size.
Dragging the ball moves its start point across the valley (w2) only. The start along the valley stays at w1 = 2.2.

blocks.text:
I reviewed all six captures. The two starting-state captures pass with minor notes, and the other four fail with major findings, so the scene should not be shown as built. All findings below can be fixed in the artifact.

**What works**
- The surface heights, the ball's height, the loss and noise readouts, the step rule and the 1/√batch noise are all computed correctly and agree with the pictures.
- At the start, both arrows are visible and point the right way (`v0-s0`, `v1-s0`).

**Major problems**
1. **The arrows disappear once the ball nears the bottom** (`v0-s1`, `v1-s1`). Both arrows are hidden: the full-batch step is about 0.04 long against a ball 0.28 wide. So the noisy-versus-true arrow comparison, which is the main idea, can't be seen for most of a run. The arrows need one larger, disclosed scale that stays readable near the bottom.
2. **The high learning rate never shows the promised back-and-forth bounce** (`v0-s2`, `v1-s2`).
   - At 0.5 the bounce repeats every 2 steps, but the trail records a point only every 3 steps. The trail draws an almost straight line instead of a zigzag.
   - The run also stops as "diverged" after only 6 steps.
   - The fix is to record the trail every step for the visible stretch, or every 2 steps at most, and let the bounce play out longer before ending the run.

**Minor notes**
- At the start, the thin full-batch arrow is mostly hidden under the thick noisy arrow.
- The surface fills a modest part of the frame, with empty space on both sides.
- The trail spacing differs from the plan (every 3 steps, up to 100 points, instead of every 5 and at most 60). This is disclosed.
- Dragging moves the start only across the valley, not to any point on the surface as planned. This is disclosed.

**Not sampled**: the batch-size options (including full batch), "Run again, keep old trail", dragging the ball, and the lowest learning rate.
